blocks.text: On entering he almost fell, for there was another step behind the door. “They show little consideration for the public,” he said. “They show no consideration at all,” said the court usher, “just look at the waiting room here.” It was a long passage, from which roughly carpentered doors led into the separate compartments of the attic. Although no light entered directly, it was not quite dark, for some of the compartments had, facing the passage, mere wooden lattices instead of solid plank walls, lattices which did, however, reach to the ceiling, through which some light penetrated and through which one could also see individual officials writing at tables or standing right by the lattice and watching the people in the passage through the gaps. There were only a few people in the passage, probably because it was Sunday. They made a very unassuming impression. At almost regular intervals they sat on the two rows of long wooden benches placed along either side of the passage. All were shabbily dressed, although most of them, to judge by their expressions, their bearing, the fashion of their beards and many small details scarcely possible to ascertain, belonged to the upper classes. As there were no coat hooks, they had put their hats beneath the bench, probably following one another’s example. When those sitting nearest the door caught sight of K. and the court usher, they rose in greeting, and when those farther along saw this, they thought they too must greet them, so that all rose as the two passed. They never stood quite upright, their backs were bent, their knees bowed, they stood like beggars in the street. K. waited for the court usher, who was walking a little behind him, and said: “How humiliated they must be.” “Yes,” said the court usher, “they are defendants, all those you see here are defendants.” “Indeed!” said K. “Then they are my colleagues.” And he turned to the nearest, a tall, slender man whose hair was already almost grey. “What are you waiting for here?” K. asked politely. But this unexpected address confused the man, which was all the more painful to see since he was plainly a man of the world, who elsewhere certainly knew how to control himself and did not lightly relinquish the superiority he had acquired over many others. Here, however, he did not know how to answer so simple a question and looked towards the others as though they were obliged to help him, and as though no one could demand an answer of him if this help were not forthcoming. Then the court usher stepped forward and said, to reassure and encourage the man: “The gentleman is only asking what you are waiting for. Do answer him.” The court usher’s voice, probably familiar to him, had a better effect: “I am waiting—” he began, and faltered. Evidently he had chosen this opening so as to answer the question in precisely the terms in which it had been put, but now could find no continuation. Some of those waiting had come closer and stood round the group; the court usher said to them: “Away, away, keep the passage clear.” They drew back a little, but not as far as their former seats. Meanwhile the man who had been questioned had collected himself and answered even with a faint smile: “A month ago I made several applications for evidence to be taken in my case, and I am waiting for them to be dealt with.” “You seem to be taking a great deal of trouble,” said K. “Yes,” said the man, “it is my case, after all.” “Not everyone thinks as you do,” said K., “I, for instance, am also accused, but as I hope for salvation, I have neither made an application for evidence to be taken nor undertaken anything else of the kind. Do you consider it necessary, then?” “I do not really know,” said the man, once more in complete uncertainty; he evidently believed that K. was making fun of him, and therefore, for fear of making some fresh mistake, he would probably have liked best to repeat his earlier answer in its entirety, but under K.’s impatient gaze he merely said, “as far as I am concerned, I have made applications for evidence to be taken.” “You probably do not believe that I am accused,” K. asked. “Oh, certainly, sir,” said the man, stepping a little aside, but there was no belief in his answer, only fear. “So you do not believe me?” K. asked, and, unconsciously prompted by the man’s humble manner, took him by the arm as though he wished to compel him to believe. He had no wish to hurt him, and had only touched him very lightly, yet the man cried out as though K. had seized him not with two fingers but with red-hot pincers. This ridiculous crying finally exhausted K.’s patience; if they did not believe that he was accused, so much the better; perhaps the man even took him for a judge. And now, by way of farewell, he really did seize him more firmly, thrust him back upon the bench and walked on. “Most defendants are so sensitive,” said the court usher. Behind them almost all those waiting were now gathering round the man, who had already ceased crying out, and seemed to be questioning him closely about the incident. A guard now came towards K., chiefly distinguishable by a sabre whose scabbard, to judge at least by its colour, was made of aluminium. K. marvelled at this and even reached out his hand towards it. The guard, who had come because of the cry, asked what had happened. The court usher sought to reassure him with a few words, but the guard declared that he must nevertheless see for himself, saluted and walked on with very hurried but very short steps, probably measured out by gout.
